articles.title: Financial Capital Didn’t Make New York City Great
articles.author: Daniel Wortel-London
articles.content_excerpt: It’s the beginning of the new Ric Burns documentary on New York City, and Adam Gopnik is choking up. He’s talking about the diversity and tolerance that New York, at its best, embodies. He’s talking about the challenges the city has faced over the past fifty years. Above all, he’s talking about how it met those challenges: through its willingness to adapt. Cities are “self-emergent” and “self-sustaining” forms, Gopnik argues, but self-sustaining requires transformation. Happily, New York has been up to the task. “We accept [New York’s] remaking of itself again and again,” he avers, and it is this tradition of demographic and developmental pluralism (“plural pluralisms,” in his inimitable phrasing) that allowed Gotham to transcend its postwar decay and become the beacon of cosmopolitan, pro

articles.title: Focus on the Real Drivers of the Affordability Crisis
articles.author: Robbie Nelson
articles.content_excerpt: Over the past five years, the price of consumer goods has dominated American political discourse. From Donald Trump to Zohran Mamdani, winning candidates have used “affordability politics” to articulate popular dissatisfaction with economic conditions. From the price of eggs to gas to burritos, the terms of discussion in the media, the campaign trail, and the proverbial kitchen table have revolved around the cost-of-living crisis embodied in these consumer goods. Although figures on the Right and center of the political scene have used inflation and affordability politics to bolster their agendas, during the second Trump administration, it is the Left and center left that have principally benefited from the salience of price talk. articles.title: Alberta’s Post-Referendum Hangover
articles.author: Laurence Miall
articles.content_excerpt: Alberta is one of the unhappiest provinces in Canada, a reminder of the old adage that money can’t buy happiness. The province fails to responsibly manage the riches from its oil and gas sector, leaving little of the spoils to Alberta workers, while billions in profits flow to foreign shareholders, many of them American. Perhaps the unhappiest of all Albertans are the separatists. This right-wing populist fringe helped push the province into a deeply divisive referendum, which failed in its aim to garner support for independence from Canada. The October 19 referendum’s very existence suggests that Premier Danielle Smith is governing with an almost exclusive focus on managing pressures within her party to protect her own leadership. articles.title: Is Ecuador Still a Democracy?
articles.author: Carlo Campo
articles.content_excerpt: “I’d be lying to you if I told you that yesterday I didn’t double-lock the door, just in case they come to take us down in the middle of the night.” Those were the words of Jahiren Noriega, a member of Ecuador’s National Assembly, the day after the detention of Luisa González, the Movimiento Revolución Ciudadana’s presidential candidate in the country’s last two federal elections and the main opposition figure today. In Ecuador, where the separation of powers no longer exists, the use of lawfare by the far-right government of President Daniel Noboa blurs the line between democracy and dictatorship. articles.title: Brazil’s Working-Class President Lula Defeats Far-Right Challenger in Run-Off Election
articles.content_excerpt: Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, universally known as “Lula,” defeated far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro on October 25 to win a fourth term. A former metalworker and union leader who led strikes in defiance of Brazil’s military dictatorship in the 1970s, Lula was elected to the presidency in 2002, 2006, and again in 2022 as the candidate of the Workers’ Party, a working-class party formed by the country’s unions in 1980. In a joint statement , Brazil’s main union federations declared that, “President Lula’s victory is a victory of hope and democracy. ... Throughout the country, demonstrations, marches, and gatherings multiplied. articles.title: Socialism Matters
articles.author: Peter McLaren
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. As the midterms loom, the question of socialism becomes increasingly urgent. We are told that we live in democracies. We vote, debate, protest, and occasionally celebrate the spectacle of our collective sovereignty. Yet for most working people, democracy stops at the factory gate, the office door, the hospital corridor, and the university's administrative suite. The decisions that shape our working lives remain concentrated in the hands of owners, executives, shareholders, and managerial elites. articles.title: Fatherland Feels Both Ancient and Tragically Contemporary
articles.author: Corey Robin
articles.content_excerpt: Fatherland , the new Paweł Pawlikowski film about Thomas Mann’s 1949 trip to Germany, may be the most powerful film about the current moment — really, the last ten years — that I’ve seen. It’s not about the current moment at all, in fact. It’s about Mann’s olympian, and doomed, effort to remain a man of culture, a voice of liberal civilization in the face of that civilization’s total collapse. In other words, it’s about the current moment. As Thomas and his daughter, Erika Mann, played by the brilliant Sandra Hüller, tour a Germany divided in two and still struggling to get back on its feet, they confront the detritus of the barbarism that has consumed Europe and the gentility of the collaborators who helped bring that barbarism about. articles.title: France’s Rulers Want Violence as a Pretext for a Crackdown
articles.author: Marlon Ettinger
articles.content_excerpt: The French government was almost desperate for something to happen. Over the weekend, the social movement that started with a series of high school blockades in mid-September continued with a well-attended, orderly march around the outskirts of Paris. The protest route, initially scheduled and approved to take place between the central Place de la Bastille and Place de la Nation, was shifted to a path between Porte d’Italie and Porte de Vincennes, a route along the southeastern rim of the city that traces the highway that encircles Paris. articles.title: Fifteen Years Later
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content_excerpt: Madrid in Winter 2026, six months before the eviction of Maricarmen (Working Mass) By : Javier Moreno Zacarés This was originally published in New Left Review on October 9, 2026. Fifteen years after the indignados occupied the Puerta del Sol, Madrid’s central plaza is once again the locus of a mass movement that has brought Spain to a political impasse. How are we back here again? The immediate trigger was the eviction of an elderly tenant. Maricarmen Abascal, who had occupied her rent-capped apartment in central Madrid since 1956, was expelled from her home on 23 September after the investment fund Urbagestión acquired the property and exploited a legal loophole to quintuple her rent.
